lesson.title: A Single Swap: Missense Mutations and Sickle Cell Disease
lesson.summary: A missense mutation changes a codon into one that specifies a different amino acid, and whether that swap matters depends on where in the protein it falls and how different the new amino acid is from the original.
lesson.body:
Where a silent mutation changes the codon but not the amino acid, a missense mutation changes both. The earlier codon example shows this too: changing the first base of UCA, serine, from U to C produces CCA, which codes for proline instead. The protein now carries proline at a position that used to hold serine, a single amino acid substitution in what may be a chain of hundreds of amino acids.

Whether that single substitution matters depends heavily on two things: where in the protein it occurs, and how chemically different the new amino acid is from the original. A conservative substitution, one where the new amino acid has similar size, shape, and charge to the one it replaces, often has little effect on how the protein folds or functions, especially if it occurs on the protein's surface, away from any active site or region that other molecules must bind. A nonconservative substitution, swapping a small nonpolar amino acid for a large charged one, for instance, is far more likely to disrupt the protein's three dimensional shape, and if it occurs in a region critical for folding or function, such as an enzyme's active site, the consequences can be severe.

The clearest real world illustration of a nonconservative missense mutation is sickle cell disease. The gene for the beta chain of hemoglobin normally has the codon GAG at position six, coding for glutamic acid, a negatively charged amino acid. A single base substitution changes this codon to GTG, which codes for valine, a nonpolar amino acid. That one substitution, out of the roughly 146 amino acids in the beta chain, is enough to change how hemoglobin molecules interact with one another under low oxygen conditions, causing them to aggregate into rigid fibers that distort red blood cells into the characteristic sickle shape. A single missense mutation, in the wrong place, can have consequences for an entire organism.

Missense mutations sit in between the two other outcomes of a point mutation in a real sense: unlike a silent mutation, they always change the protein's sequence, but unlike a nonsense mutation, they never stop translation early, so the rest of the protein downstream of the change is made normally. Whether that trade off is harmless, mildly altering, or as consequential as the sickle cell mutation depends entirely on the specific amino acids involved and where in the protein the change occurs.
